# Putting data to good use {#gooduse}

## Failure mode

I hope to have shown that the data in @WalkdenEa2023 do not provide strong evidence for the authors' claims, though the authors plainly believe they do. How did that happen? The shape of the mistake is by now familiar. A loosely specified theory (Section \@ref(hypotheses)) was asked to draw support from a chain of derivations --- substantive tenets to particular predictions to statistical hypotheses to Nulls of the form "*variable V has no influence*" --- and a positive inference was then run all the way back up the chain, from "the Null is rejected" to "Trudgill's theory is corroborated and our method works." Each step treated every auxiliary hypothesis in the network as true and every rejected Null as a finding.

The chain breaks at both ends. At the top, the loose fit of an informal theory means even a clean rejection transmits almost nothing upward.
The test had no real capacity to find the theory wrong, so passing it is not severity but coincidence (Section \@ref(testing)). At the bottom, the rejections themselves are unsound.
They are products of NHST applied to aggregated, unweighted scores, so there is nothing to transmit in the first place.
The result is not a modest finding, or a weak one, but no finding at all. I could only speculate why none of this was caught by the authors, the editors, or the reviewers. Rather than dwell there, I offer three remedies that would help, none of them mine, as other fields have met the same problems and thought hard about them.

## Remedy 1: disciplined inference and better theories

Be modest about what an inference can carry. Testing is piecemeal, and any one study should aim at the most specific corner of the hypothesis network it can actually reach, not the grand theory above it. The deeper fix, though, is on the theory side.
Linguistic theories would be far more testable if they predicted *numbers* or at minimum a numerical range the measurements should fall in. That is what sharpens a particular hypothesis into something a test can genuinely fail. Where a research tradition measures the same thing repeatedly, those ranges can also come from meta-analysis [see @Vasishth2015 for a rare example of meta-analysis in linguistics, albeit from psycholinguistics].

With numerical expectations in hand, one can sharpen tests using Neyman--Pearson logic [@NeymanPearson1933; @Neyman1937; @Neyman1957] or severity [@MayoSpanos2004] and earn a real positive inference, rather than merely rejecting an uninformative Null. But we should be honest about the catch. Principled confirmatory testing needs not only numerical predictions but data of sufficient quantity, control, and quality to put them at risk. Historical-corpus data of the kind Walkden et al. work with will, in all likelihood, never meet that bar.
There simply are not, and never will be, enough well-controlled texts from the right places and centuries. Recognising when the data cannot bear *any* confirmatory framework is itself part of disciplined inference. The answer is not to run Neyman--Pearson or any approach to inferential statistics harder, but it is to stop forcing data into a method of inference not made for them.

And, maybe, the field also needs higher standards of statistical training.
We should treat applied statistics as a core skill of the discipline, taught properly, rather than a bolt-on.

## Remedy 2: open data as part of the review process

Reviewers and editors can only catch what they can see. A look at the underlying data should be a standard part of review, and reviewers should be equipped to make use of it. The clues in @WalkdenEa2023 as published are real but partial. The actual problems surface only on reanalysis, once one actually engages with the data set. In my experience also as an author, reviewers even at empirically minded journals rarely catch design or analysis errors, whether for want of the data or for want of the time to look.
Behind this sits a missing standard. Most journals might still accept anything that reports a GLM (in the spirit of the diverse empirical and quantitative turns) without having established clear standards for the reporting of such statistical methods.
Authors and reviewers can then impose whatever checks suit their taste. A journal with no best-practice guidelines for statistical methods arguably should not be publishing papers that lean on them at all, unless the paper's own contribution is purely methodological and the paper is instrumental in establishing such guidelines.

## Remedy 3: negative findings and preregistration

The pressure to publish, and to publish positive findings, is the often mourned underlying cause of the whole problem [@Ioannidis2005; @SimmonsEa2011].
One answer to that is preregistration [@Lakens2019; @Boettger2021].
The study's motivation and design are submitted and judged before it is conducted, and the paper is published on the strength of the design whatever the results turn out to be. That makes negative findings publishable and gives researchers room to be hard on their own data. However, on its own preregistration might not be the perfect cure. Negative results draw few citations, so the incentive to find something publishable survives, as does the temptation to wave a good-looking result through without inspecting the data or the model.
Recent work in other fields suggests preregistration has to be done exactly right to curb the practices the positive-results pressure encourages, see @BrodeurEa2024.

I close on a constructive note rather than a sour one. Philology traditionally is a discipline of careful close reading, aimed at understanding texts in their linguistic and cultural setting.
For good reason, it felt no obligation to the apparatus of the scientific method or to large-scale statistics. One reason was simply that the textual record is often too thin, across the relevant times and places, to support reliable statistical inference. Furthermore, individual sentences or even words in historic sources might require a careful interpretation (close reading) not recoverable with data-driven methods where sentences and words become mere data points.
I ask readers to consider whether that has really changed.
It is worth asking why a confirmatory inferential quantitative analysis should be reached for where a philological reading would serve better.

However, none of this is a brief against data analysis per se.
Given the aforementioned problems with historical data sources, the distinction that matters is the one Study 1 already turned on.
Describing a sample is one thing, inferring to a population another, and inferring to a causal network of hypotheses something else again. Exploratory data analysis is a genuine and valuable tool, but its goals are orthogonal to any testing framework, principled (like Neyman-Pearson) or otherwise (NHST).
It asks what is in the data, not whether a theory survives. Read that way, the data of @WalkdenEa2023 should be put to good use. What is problematic about the paper is not the data but the confirmatory burden placed on them.
We should match the instrument to what the data can bear, be it close reading, exploration, or, where the data genuinely allow, a severe test.
